content: Coercivity, also referred to as the coercive field, is a property of ferromagnetic materials that quantifies the strength of the external magnetic field required to reduce the material's magnetization to zero after it has been magnetically saturated. This property is typically expressed in units such as oersted or ampere per meter and is symbolized as ( H_C ). When a ferromagnetic material exhibits a high coercive field, it is classified as a hard or permanent magnet. Permanent magnets are widely utilized in applications such as electric motors, magnetic recording media (e.g., hard drives, floppy disks, and magnetic tapes), and magnetic separation systems. Conversely, ferromagnetic materials with low coercive fields are considered soft and are often employed in devices like microwave components, magnetic shielding, transformers, and recording heads. The coercivity of a material can be experimentally determined using a B-H Analyzer. This is typically achieved using instruments such as vibrating-sample magnetometers or alternating-gradient magnetometers. The coercivity corresponds to the value of the applied magnetic field at which the magnetization curve crosses zero. This phenomenon, known as magnetic creep, occurs when the reversal of magnetization via domain wall motion is thermally activated and influenced by magnetic viscosity. At high frequencies, the increasing coercivity poses a significant challenge to achieving higher data rates in magnetic recording systems, especially since higher storage densities often necessitate materials with greater coercivity. At the coercive field, the component of the magnetization vector aligned with the applied magnetic field becomes zero. Magnetization reversal in ferromagnetic materials occurs through two primary mechanisms: rotation and domain wall motion. When magnetization reverses via rotation, the magnetization vector becomes orthogonal to the applied field, resulting in a zero component along the field direction. In contrast, when reversal occurs through domain wall motion, the net magnetization in all vector directions is effectively zero because the magnetic moments of individual domains cancel each other out. Magnetization curves dominated by rotation and magnetocrystalline anisotropy are typically observed in highly uniform magnetic materials used in fundamental research. However, in practical engineering materials, domain wall motion is the predominant mechanism of magnetization reversal. This is because structural defects, such as grain boundaries and impurities, act as nucleation sites for reversed-magnetization domains. The behavior of domain walls in determining coercivity is complex, as defects can both pin and nucleate domain walls. The dynamics of domain walls in ferromagnetic materials share similarities with the behavior of grain boundaries and plastic deformation in metallurgy, as both involve planar defects. The area enclosed within the magnetization curve during a single cycle represents the work done on the magnet. Common dissipative processes in magnetic materials include magnetostriction and domain wall motion. For soft magnetic materials, coercivity serves as an indicator of their energy loss characteristics in practical applications. For hard magnetic materials, figures of merit include the squareness ratio (( M(H=0)/M_s )) and coercivity, although the energy product (the product of saturation magnetization and coercivity) is often the most cited parameter. In the 1980s, rare-earth boride magnets with high energy products were developed, but these materials exhibited undesirably low Curie temperatures. Since the 1990s, advancements have led to the creation of exchange-spring hard magnets, which combine high coercivities with improved performance characteristics.
